summary: CDDL is a notation for describing the shape of CBOR and JSON data, and it can be extended with "control operators". This RFC adds several general-purpose ones for converting between bytes, integers, and text, for printf-style formatting, and for JSON. They let a schema say that one piece of text is derived from another value.

eli5.summary: Imagine a form that says "this box must be the number above, written out in words." This adds new rules like that to a language for describing what data should look like.

questions: cddl control operators for text conversion
how to describe json text in cddl
what is a cddl control operator
how to model base64 text in cddl
subtitle: New CDDL control operators that let a data schema describe text made from bytes, numbers, JSON or joined pieces.

tldr.problem: CDDL schemas often need to say that a text string is really something else in disguise, such as base64 text for a byte string or a number written in decimal. The existing control operators did not cover these common cases.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines new control operators: base-encoding operators (.b64u, .b64c, .hex, .b32, .h32, .b45 and variants), .base10 for integers, .printf for printf-style formatting, .json for embedded JSON, and .join for concatenating array elements into a string.
tldr.outcome: Schema authors can model text conversions directly in CDDL. The operators were registered in the IANA CDDL Control Operators registry.

today: RFC 9741 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Control Operators as the Extension Point
sections.content:
CDDL (Concise Data Definition Language) is standardized in RFC 8610. Its main extension point is the control operator, which ties a target type on the left to a controller on the right. Earlier RFCs added operators in an application-specific way (RFC 9090) and a more general way (RFC 9165).

This document adds more generally applicable operators. Its Table 1 lists them with the target type (t) and controller type (c): the base-encoding operators take text targets and bytes controllers, .base10 takes int, .printf takes an array, .json takes any, and .join takes an array and works on text or bytes.

The RFC calls its choices opinionated: it picks the combinations it expects to be used, and leaving one out does not mean it is unacceptable. It might be added later.
sections.eli5: A control operator is a small extra rule you can attach to a data description, like "and it must be written this way." This document hands out a new box of those rules.

sections.title: Byte Strings as Base16, Base32, Base45 and Base64 Text
sections.content:
A model often describes data that is really a byte string but travels as text, for example in JSON. The operators here model that conversion. A typical use is signature-for-json = text .b64u signature where signature = bytes .cbor COSE_Sign1.

The names follow RFC 4648 plus RFC 9285 for Base45: .b64u (base64url, no padding), .b64c (classic base64, padding), .b32 (base32, no padding), .h32 (base32 with the Extended Hex alphabet, no padding), .hex (base16, either case), .hexlc (lower case), .hexuc (upper case) and .b45.

The operators are strict: they only match encodings that conform to their defining documents. So .b64u and .b64c each accept only their own alphabet, unlike the b64 literal prefix in CDDL source, which accepts characters from either alphabet.

The RFC is opinionated here. It does not offer base64url or base32(hex) with padding, or classic base64 without padding, because experience indicates these combinations only occur in error. The c in .b64c makes sure that choosing classic base64 is a deliberate decision.

The sloppy variants, .b64u-sloppy and .b64c-sloppy, do not check that the extra trailing bits are zero. No sloppy variant of base32 or base32hex is defined because no legacy use was known. Base45 is known to be suboptimal in environments with limited data transparency such as URLs, but it is included because of its close relationship to QR codes and its wide use in health informatics. It is strongly specified not to allow sloppy forms.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a secret code made of numbers has to be written out using only letters so it can go in a text message. These rules say which letter-writing style is allowed, and they are picky about it.

sections.title: Integers and Printf-Style Formatting
sections.content:
.base10 models a text string that holds an integer in ordinary decimal digits, such as the uint64 and int64 formats of YANG-JSON (RFC 7951). The example is yang-json-sid = text .base10 (0..9223372036854775807). Only numerals without leading zeros match, that is, the regular expression 0|-?[1-9][0-9]*, further limited by the controller type. The name spells out "base" so it is not confused with the byte-string operators such as .b64u.

.printf handles formats that C-style printf can produce, including other bases such as octal, hexadecimal or binary. The controller is an array holding one format string followed by zero or more data items. The construct matches a text string equal to the output of the equivalent C printf call.

Some printf features are excluded. Length modifiers MUST NOT appear in the format string, and neither may the p and n conversion specifiers. The s specifier interpolates a UTF-8 text string, and c stands for a single Unicode scalar value as a UTF-8 character.

For example, hexlabel<K> = text .printf (["0x%04x", K]) makes hexlabel<19> match the text "0x0013". The data items need not be literals: hexlabel<1..20> matches "0x0013" or "0x0001" but not "0x1234".
sections.eli5: One rule says a number must be written in plain digits with no extra zeros on the front. The other rule is a fill-in-the-blanks template, like "0x" followed by a four-digit number.

sections.title: Text That Contains JSON
sections.content:
Some applications store a complete JSON text inside a text string. The .json operator models this. It works like the .cbor operator of RFC 8610, using the default JSON-to-CBOR conversion rules from RFC 8949. The example is embedded-claims = text .json claims with claims = {iss: text, exp: text}.

The RFC adds notes:

  • JSON has known interoperability problems (RFC 7493). Following Section 2 of that RFC is needed to use CDDL's generic data model, and the advice to carry numbers outside JSON's interoperable range as text strings must be reflected on the right-hand side of .json.
  • The operator cannot constrain blank space or other serialization variants, such as the order of map entries. Future control operators could define such restrictions.
  • No .jsonseq for JSON text sequences (RFC 7464) is provided, since no use case was known at the time of writing.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a whole note written in one format is tucked inside a box of another format. This rule lets you describe what the tucked-in note must look like.

sections.title: Building Text with .join
sections.content:
.join models text built from parts that are best described as an array. The elements of the controller array must be strings (text or byte strings). The operator matches a string that is the concatenation of those elements. The result is the same kind of string as the first element, and an empty array matches either kind of empty string, subject to the target. Concatenation works on bytes, and a text result must be valid UTF-8, although the individual pieces do not each have to be valid text.

The RFC's example builds a dotted-decimal IPv4 address from four .base10 numbers between 0 and 255, joined by "." markers.

.join is hard to validate in the most general case because that would need full parser functionality. The RFC recommends limiting it to simple arrangements where elements are laid out explicitly, no variable elements are adjacent without a constant between them, and the constants do not occur within the text the variable elements describe.

For validators, an implementation note suggests using the constant markers to isolate variable parts, or building a parsing regular expression with a capture group per element. It RECOMMENDS full coverage at least for the marker-based subset. For harder parsing, the ABNF control operators of RFC 9165 may help, but they cannot reach back into CDDL elements the way .join can.
sections.eli5: It is like gluing word cards together to make a sentence. You list the cards in order, and the rule says the final text must be exactly all of them stuck together.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has registered fourteen names in the CDDL Control Operators registry, each pointing to RFC 9741: .b64u, .b64u-sloppy, .b64c, .b64c-sloppy, .b45, .b32, .h32, .hex, .hexlc, .hexuc, .base10, .printf, .json and .join.
sections.eli5: The new rule names were written in an official list so nobody else picks the same names for something different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The section is short. The security considerations of Section 5 of RFC 8610 apply. For the byte-string operators of Section 2.1, the security considerations in Section 12 of RFC 4648 apply as well.
sections.eli5: The safety advice from the older rulebooks still applies to these new rules, so read those too.

data.code:

legacy-ip-address-elements = [bytetext, ".", bytetext, ".",
                              bytetext, ".", bytetext]
bytetext = text .base10 byte
byte = 0..255
